Growth distributions: quantile models, growth inequality and conditional references

Source: vignettes/growth-distributions.Rmd
growth-distributions.Rmd

About this vignette. All data are simulated with wgh_simulate(). The results show how the methods work and resemble the published patterns, but they are not the published findings and are not research results. The functions run in development mode, with 50 bootstrap replicates for the quantile models and 5-fold cross-validation for the references.

Means hide what happens at the edges of a distribution. A child at the 5th centile of height and a child at the 95th may respond differently to the same BMI. This vignette shows three ways of modelling the whole distribution, each from a study of the research program:

  1. how BMI relates to height-for-age at different quantiles and ages, with quantile regression and linear quantile mixed models (Ho 2026) [1],
  2. how the spread of height-for-age changes with BMI and age, a measure of growth inequality (Ho 2026) [2], and
  3. conditional growth references, which say where a child is expected to be at a later age given the child’s own earlier growth (Ho 2026) [3].

The vignette is precomputed.

library(WeGrowHealthR)
wgh_config("dev")
#> WeGrowHealthR run mode: dev
v <- wgh_simulate(30000, seed = 2026)$visits
fl <- wgh_sample_flow(v, "Ages 5 to 18" = ~ age >= 5 & age <= 18.5,
                      "Plausible z-scores" = ~ abs(haz) < 6 & abs(baz) < 6,
                      "At least 3 visits" = wgh_min_visits(3))
a <- fl$data
girls <- a[a$sex == "Female", ]
boys <- a[a$sex == "Male", ]

1. Quantile regression of HAZ on BAZ

The model lets the association of BAZ with HAZ change smoothly with age, through a natural spline of age interacting with BAZ:

f <- haz ~ splines::ns(age, knots = c(8, 11, 14), Boundary.knots = c(5, 18.5)) * baz

Write the knots and boundary knots into the formula. If they were chosen from the data, every bootstrap replicate would get a slightly different basis and the replicates could not be combined.

wgh_rq() fits the model at each quantile in taus, reads the BAZ slope at the anchor_ages by contrast (the change in predicted HAZ when BAZ rises by one unit at that age), and gets intervals from a bootstrap that resamples children (B replicates), so repeated visits are handled correctly.

fit_g <- wgh_rq(girls, f, taus = c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95), anchor_ages = c(6, 9, 12, 15), B = 50)
fit_g
#> <wgh_rq>: 5 quantiles, 15628 visits from 3827 children, 50 bootstrap replicates
#> Slope of baz by age and quantile:
#> # A tibble: 20 x 6
#>      age   tau estimate boot_se  lower  upper
#>    <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>

#>  2     9  0.05    0.096   0.019  0.066  0.131
#>  3    12  0.05    0.036   0.021  0.005  0.084
#>  4    15  0.05   -0.09    0.039 -0.149 -0.004

#>  6     9  0.25    0.167   0.015  0.131  0.193

#>  8    15  0.25   -0.034   0.022 -0.074  0.012

#> 10     9  0.5     0.166   0.013  0.147  0.197
#> 11    12  0.5     0.083   0.016  0.062  0.115
#> 12    15  0.5     0.032   0.018 -0.002  0.064
#> 13     6  0.75    0.153   0.019  0.132  0.193

The printout gives the BAZ slope at each age and quantile with its bootstrap standard error and interval. The same table is in fit_g$slopes.

plot(fit_g, y_label = "Change in HAZ per unit BAZ")

Before puberty the slope is positive and largest at the upper quantiles: higher BMI goes with greater height, most of all among the tallest girls. By 15 years the slope is close to zero in the middle of the distribution and negative at the 5th centile, the same convergence seen in vignette("trajectories").

wgh_test_heterogeneity() tests whether the slopes at one age are equal across quantiles, and wgh_test_sex_difference() whether boys and girls differ:

fit_b <- wgh_rq(boys, f, taus = c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95), anchor_ages = c(6, 9, 12, 15), B = 50)
wgh_test_heterogeneity(fit_g, age = 12)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 7
#>     age chi_sq    df  p_value top_minus_bottom lower upper
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>            <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    12   72.4     4 6.99e-15            0.210 0.142 0.248
wgh_test_sex_difference(fit_b, fit_g, age = 12)$joint
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>     age chi_sq    df  p_value
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <int>    <dbl>
#> 1    12   25.0     5 0.000139

wgh_slopes() reads slopes at any other ages from the same fit, for example wgh_slopes(fit_g, ages = c(7, 13)).

Accounting for repeated visits: LQMM

Quantile regression treats visits as independent and handles clustering only through the bootstrap. A linear quantile mixed model adds a random intercept for each child. wgh_lqmm() has the same interface as wgh_rq() and retries with more iterations when the optimiser warns.

set.seed(1)
small <- girls[girls$id %in% sample(unique(girls$id), 600), ]
lq <- wgh_lqmm(small, f, taus = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), anchor_ages = c(6, 9, 12, 15), B = 0)
lq$slopes
#> # A tibble: 12 x 3
#>      age   tau estimate
#>    <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1     6   0.1   0.0745
#>  2     9   0.1   0.135 
#>  3    12   0.1   0.105 
#>  4    15   0.1   0.0181
#>  5     6   0.5   0.154 
#>  6     9   0.5   0.266 
#>  7    12   0.5   0.163 
#>  8    15   0.5   0.0344
#>  9     6   0.9   0.0203
#> 10     9   0.9   0.0821
#> 11    12   0.9  -0.0102
#> 12    15   0.9  -0.118
lq$convergence
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>     tau ok    converged ladder_step method messages
#>   <dbl> <lgl> <lgl>           <dbl> <chr>  <chr>   
#> 1   0.1 TRUE  TRUE                1 gs     ""      
#> 2   0.5 TRUE  TRUE                1 gs     ""      
#> 3   0.9 TRUE  TRUE                1 gs     ""

The convergence table reports, for each quantile, whether the fit converged, which step of the retry ladder was needed and the messages of the failed attempts.

2. Growth inequality: the spread of height-for-age

The same quantile model describes the spread of the distribution. The distance between the 95th and the 5th centile of HAZ (range90) and the interquartile range (iqr) can be read at any age and BAZ. wgh_dispersion() does that, with bootstrap intervals, and also reports the change in spread per unit of BAZ.

dsp <- wgh_dispersion(fit_g, ages = c(6, 9, 12, 15), exposure_values = c(-1, 0, 1, 2, 3))
head(dsp$spread)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 8
#>     age   baz range90   iqr range90_lower range90_upper iqr_lower iqr_upper
#>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1     6    -1    2.09 0.857          1.98          2.22     0.794     0.903
#> 2     9    -1    1.97 0.723          1.89          2.08     0.665     0.763
#> 3    12    -1    1.87 0.798          1.78          1.99     0.751     0.842
#> 4    15    -1    1.79 0.751          1.66          1.92     0.676     0.825
#> 5     6     0    2.28 0.915          2.20          2.35     0.865     0.954
#> 6     9     0    2.16 0.810          2.10          2.24     0.770     0.850
dsp$change
#> # A tibble: 4 x 7
#>     age range90_per_unit iqr_per_unit range90_lower range90_upper iqr_lower iqr_upper
#>   <dbl>            <dbl>        <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1     6            0.189       0.0573        0.107          0.243   0.0138     0.0951
#> 2     9            0.185       0.0867        0.142          0.234   0.0656     0.115 
#> 3    12            0.210       0.0375        0.142          0.248   0.00278    0.0667
#> 4    15            0.210       0.0693        0.0759         0.269   0.0157     0.108

A spread read at a BAZ where few children are measured is an extrapolation. wgh_support() counts the children near each age and BAZ and flags the supported cells:

sup <- wgh_support(girls, "baz", ages = c(6, 9, 12, 15), exposure_values = c(-1, 0, 1, 2, 3))
head(sup)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 4
#>     age   baz n_local supported
#>   <dbl> <dbl>   <int> <lgl>    
#> 1     6    -1     107 TRUE     
#> 2     9    -1     162 TRUE     
#> 3    12    -1      88 TRUE     
#> 4    15    -1      82 TRUE     
#> 5     6     0     200 TRUE     
#> 6     9     0     282 TRUE
sp <- merge(dsp$spread, sup[, c("age", "baz", "supported")], by = c("age", "baz"))
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(sp[sp$supported, ], aes(baz, range90, colour = factor(age))) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = range90_lower, ymax = range90_upper), width = 0.1) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_colour_wgh() + theme_wgh() +
  labs(x = "BMI-for-age z-score", y = "HAZ P95 minus P5", colour = "Age")

In these simulated girls the spread widens by about 0.2 HAZ units for each unit of BAZ at every age (dsp$change): girls with higher BMI differ more from each other in height than girls with normal BMI, a form of growth inequality that a mean model cannot show.

3. Conditional growth references

A WHO chart compares a child with all children of the same age and sex. A conditional reference compares the child with children who had the same starting point. It answers a clinical question: given this child’s height and BMI at 6 years, where should the child’s height-for-age be at 10, 12 or 14 years? A child who stays inside the WHO band can still fall well below the course expected from the child’s own history, and that is what a conditional reference detects.

A cohort with long follow-up

Conditional references need children measured both in a conditioning window and years later. The simulation settings below give a cohort followed for 14 school years with little dropout: years sets the calendar years, dropout the yearly probability of leaving, and entry_first_prob the share of children enrolled from their first eligible year.

long <- wgh_simulate(12000, preset = "reference", seed = 11, years = 2012:2025,
                     dropout = c(intercept = -4, age = 0), entry_first_prob = 0.9)$visits

Building the panel

wgh_conditional_panel() takes, for each child, the visit nearest anchor (6 years) within the conditioning window as the baseline, a second visit near anchor2 for a slope, and the visit nearest each target age (within tol years) as the outcome. Children are not dropped for lacking the second visit.

cp <- wgh_conditional_panel(long, window = c(5, 9), anchor = 6, anchor2 = 8, targets = c(10, 12, 14))
table(cp$sex, cp$target_nominal)
#>         
#>            10   12   14
#>   Male   1071  647  267
#>   Female  978  650  285
head(cp[, c("id", "sex", "baseline_age", "baseline_haz", "baseline_baz", "target_nominal", "target_age", "target")])
#> # A tibble: 6 x 8
#>   id      sex    baseline_age baseline_haz baseline_baz target_nominal target_age target
#>   <chr>   <fct>         <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 C000004 Male           5.53        2.82         0.314             10       9.56  1.93 
#> 2 C000005 Male           7.11       -0.126       -0.486             10      10.2  -0.659
#> 3 C000007 Male           5.92        1.44         1.74              10       9.83  0.696
#> 4 C000010 Male           5.72        0.218        0.164             10      10.5  -0.071
#> 5 C000011 Male           5.53        1.05         0.632             10      10.4   1.17 
#> 6 C000014 Female         6.42       -0.973        0.955             10      10.3  -0.088

Fitting the references

wgh_condref() fits quantile regressions of the target HAZ on the baseline features, by sex and target age, over a grid of quantiles. The formula sets the baseline features (default baseline HAZ, BAZ and age). Three benchmarks are stored alongside: the unconditional reference (the target distribution ignoring the baseline), persistence (baseline plus the typical change) and the WHO band (standard normal quantiles).

cr <- wgh_condref(cp)
cr
#> <wgh_condref>: 6 sex-by-target models, 9 quantiles
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   sex    target     n
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Male       10  1071
#> 2 Female     10   978
#> 3 Male       12   647
#> 4 Female     12   650
#> 5 Male       14   267
#> 6 Female     14   285

predict() returns the predicted quantiles for any child, under the conditional model or a benchmark (type):

child <- cp[cp$target_nominal == 14 & cp$baseline_haz < -1, ][1, ]
round(predict(cr, child), 2)
#>      q0.030 q0.050 q0.100 q0.250 q0.500 q0.750 q0.900 q0.950 q0.970
#> [1,]  -2.35  -2.32  -2.21  -2.02  -1.56  -0.93  -0.56  -0.38  -0.33
round(predict(cr, child, type = "who"), 2)
#>      q0.030 q0.050 q0.100 q0.250 q0.500 q0.750 q0.900 q0.950 q0.970
#> [1,]  -1.88  -1.64  -1.28  -0.67      0   0.67   1.28   1.64   1.88

For this child, who started below -1 HAZ, the conditional range at 14 years is centred well below zero, near the child’s own level, and is much narrower than the WHO range.

Showing one child: the fan chart

wgh_plot_fan() draws the expected course. The fan opens at the baseline measurement (known, so it has no width) and widens to the predicted 25th to 75th and 5th to 95th centile ranges at each target age. The grey band is the WHO -2 to +2 SD range, show_unconditional = TRUE adds the cohort’s unconditional range, and observed overlays the child’s later measurements.

Here is a child whose height-for-age drifted downwards. We find such a child with wgh_condref_centile() (next section): flagged below the conditional 3rd centile at 14 years, yet still inside the WHO band.

sc <- wgh_condref_centile(cr, cp)
full <- names(which(table(cp$id) == 3))
drift <- sc[sc$target_nominal == 14 & sc$cond_flag == "below" & sc$target > -2 & sc$id %in% full, ][1, ]
drift[, c("id", "sex", "baseline_age", "baseline_haz", "target", "cond_centile")]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   id      sex   baseline_age baseline_haz target cond_centile
#>   <chr>   <fct>        <dbl>        <dbl>  <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 C001571 Male          6.17       -0.596  -1.81         3.00
later <- long[long$pid == drift$id & long$age > drift$baseline_age, c("age", "haz")]
wgh_plot_fan(cr, drift, observed = later, show_unconditional = TRUE,
             title = "A child drifting below the expected course")

Every measurement of this child stays inside the WHO band, so a standard growth chart raises no alarm. The conditional fan shows that the child started inside the expected course and left it, which is the signal a clinician would want to see. For contrast, a child growing as expected:

typ <- sc[sc$target_nominal == 14 & abs(sc$cond_centile - 50) < 10 & sc$id %in% full, ][1, ]
later_t <- long[long$pid == typ$id & long$age > typ$baseline_age, c("age", "haz")]
wgh_plot_fan(cr, typ, observed = later_t, title = "A child growing along the expected course")

Conditional centiles and flags

wgh_condref_centile() places each observed target value in its predicted distribution. cond_centile is the conditional centile (0 to 100), cond_z its normal score, and cond_flag is "below" or "above" when the centile is outside 3 to 97 (flag).

table(sc$target_nominal, sc$cond_flag)
#>     
#>      above below within
#>   10    60    61   1928
#>   12    39    39   1219
#>   14    15    18    519
# children inside the WHO band but outside their own expected range
mean(abs(sc$target) < 2 & sc$cond_flag != "within", na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.05207799

Are the references any good?

A reference is useful if its ranges are both honest and narrow. wgh_condref_cv() fits the references on part of the children and scores them on the others (folds child-level folds, or folds = "site" to leave one site out):

  • crps (continuous ranked probability score) and wis (weighted interval score) measure the accuracy of the whole predicted distribution. Lower is better.
  • coverage_90 is the share of children inside the predicted 90% range. It should be close to 0.90.
  • width_90 is the width of that range. Narrower is more useful, as long as coverage holds.
cv <- wgh_condref_cv(cp, folds = 5)
aggregate(cbind(crps, wis, coverage_90, width_90) ~ model, data = cv, FUN = mean)
#>           model      crps       wis coverage_90 width_90
#> 1   conditional 0.2318450 0.1925505   0.8888939 1.330110
#> 2   persistence 0.2919781 0.2450583   0.8960622 1.769993
#> 3 unconditional 0.5573599 0.4627864   0.8961755 3.308607
#> 4           who 0.5589127 0.4642847   0.8903847 3.289707

All four references cover about 90% of children, so all are honest. The conditional reference has by far the lowest CRPS and WIS and a 90% range less than half as wide as the WHO range: it says much more about each child for the same honesty. Persistence is in between, because it uses the baseline but ignores BMI and regression to the mean.

A flexible benchmark and a child-by-child comparison

Is the linear conditional reference too simple? A quantile random forest (wgh_quantile_forest(), built on ranger) makes no assumption about the shape of the relationship, so it is a demanding benchmark (Book 2 Chapter 15). forest = TRUE adds it to the cross-validation.

Comparing average scores across models ignores that the models predict the same children. wgh_condref_compare() scores every held-out prediction and compares two references child by child, with a bootstrap that resamples children (wgh_paired_scores(), Book 2 Chapter 16). A negative difference means the model scores better than the reference.

cmp <- wgh_condref_compare(cp, models = c("conditional", "persistence", "forest"), reference = "who",
                           folds = 5, B = 500)
cmp[, c("model", "reference", "mean_new", "mean_old", "mean_diff", "lower", "upper", "relative_change_pct")]
#> # A tibble: 3 x 8
#>   model       reference mean_new mean_old mean_diff  lower  upper relative_change_pct
#>   <chr>       <chr>        <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 conditional who          0.218    0.566    -0.348 -0.365 -0.331               -61.5
#> 2 persistence who          0.276    0.566    -0.290 -0.310 -0.271               -51.2
#> 3 forest      who          0.243    0.566    -0.322 -0.340 -0.306               -57.0
wgh_condref_compare(cp, models = "forest", reference = "conditional", folds = 5, B = 500)[,
  c("model", "reference", "mean_diff", "lower", "upper", "relative_change_pct")]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 6
#>   model  reference   mean_diff  lower  upper relative_change_pct
#>   <chr>  <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 forest conditional    0.0256 0.0214 0.0300                11.7

The first table shows how much each reference improves on the WHO band for the same children. The second asks whether the forest improves on the linear conditional reference. When its interval lies above zero the forest is worse, and the simpler linear model, which can be written as an equation and explained, is preferred.

wgh_plot_condref_calibration() checks every quantile, not only the 90% range, with out-of-fold predictions. Points on the diagonal mean that, for example, 10% of children fall below the predicted 10th centile.

wgh_plot_condref_calibration(cp, folds = 5)

engine = "lqmm" (default) uses linear quantile mixed models as in the study, and sensitivity = TRUE adds a smooth quantile regression check with qgam. Both are slower.

Where to go next

  • vignette("prediction") explains individual conditional predictions with SHAP values.
  • vignette("phenotypes-states") looks at movement between height bands over time.
